claim: TALENs targeting exon 4 of the kif5aa open reading frame generated two loss-of-function alleles with a 10 bp and 13 bp deletion, respectively.
source: Employing TALENs targeting exon4 of the kif5aa open reading frame, we generated two loss-of-function alleles with a 10 bp and 13 bp deletion, respectively.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the deletions.

claim: The kif5aa deletions result in a frameshift at amino acid 122 and a premature stop codon after 162 of 1033 amino acids within the motor domain of Kif5aa.
source: These result in a frameshift at amino acid 122 and a premature stop codon after 162 of 1033aas within the motor domain of Kif5aa.
evidence: The text explicitly states the frameshift position and premature stop codon location, supported by Figure 1A diagram.

claim: In situ hybridization shows a substantial downregulation of kif5aa mRNA in 24 hpf and 72 hpf old embryos.
source: In situ hybridization shows a substantial downregulation of kif5aa mRNA in 24 hpf and 72 hpf old embryos.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing in situ hybridization images.

claim: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR shows that only 47% of wild-type kif5aa mRNA expression levels are reached in homozygote mutant embryos at 4 dpf.
source: Quantitative reverse transcription PCR confirms that only 47% of wild-type kif5aa mRNA expression levels are reached in homozygote mutant embryos at 4 dpf (p < 0.01).
evidence: The text explicitly states the percentage and statistical significance, supported by Figure 1C showing qRT-PCR data.

claim: Kif5aa mutant embryos show expanded melanosomes within their melanocytes and appear dark compared to wild-type embryos.
source: Kif5aa mutant embryos show expanded melanosomes within their melanocytes and appear dark compared to wild-type embryos.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the phenotype and Figure 1D shows images comparing wild-type and mutant embryos.

claim: Kif5aa mutant embryos fail to inflate their swim bladder and die 10 days post fertilization.
source: They fail to inflate their swim bladder and die 10 days post fertilization.
evidence: The text explicitly states the swim bladder phenotype and lethality, supported by Figure 1E showing images.

claim: The kif5aa mutation is recessive and completely penetrant.
source: In a clutch of 5 day post-fertilization (dpf) zebrafish larvae, derived from a cross of two heterozygous carriers of the kif5aa*162 allele, 25% of the larvae exhibited a dark coloration in comparison to their wild-type siblings (Figure 1D), indicating that the mutation is recessive, completely penetrant and results in a failure to adapt to a light background by melanosome re-distribution.
evidence: The text explicitly states the mutation is recessive and completely penetrant based on Mendelian ratios observed.

claim: The optokinetic response was absent in kif5aa mutants while present in all wild-type fish examined.
source: We found that the OKR was absent in kif5aa mutants (n = 6), while it was present in all wild-type fish examined (n = 6) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The text explicitly states the OKR results with sample sizes, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1D showing eye position traces.

claim: The disruption of kif5aa causes blindness.
source: This suggests that the disruption of kif5aa causes blindness.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the absence of OKR.

claim: Application of norepinephrine results in aggregation of melanosomes in kif5aa mutant embryos.
source: Kif5aa mutant embryos were treated with norepinephrin resulting in aggregation of melanosomes and consecutive re-expansion upon washing out of the drug ([Wagle et al., 2011], Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the experimental result, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing images and citing previous work.

claim: Melanosome transport inside melanocytes in both antero- and retrograde direction is not affected in kif5aa mutant embryos.
source: This indicates that melanosome transport inside melanocytes in both antero- and retrograde direction is not affected in kif5aa mutant embryos.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the norepinephrine experiment results.

claim: The onset of retinal neurogenesis is not altered in kif5aa mutant embryos.
source: In mutant embryos, we could not observe alterations neither in the onset of retinal neurogenesis (characterized by sonic hedgehog expression [Shkumatava et al., 2004]) nor in the later specification of RGCs or other retinal cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states no alterations were observed, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing shh:eGFP expression and citing previous work.

claim: Choroid fissure and optic stalk formation are normal in kif5aa mutant embryos as revealed by the expression of pax2.1.
source: Choroid fissure and optic stalk formation, as well as rostral-caudal patterning, were normal as revealed by the expression of pax2.1 and tag-1, respectively.
evidence: The text explicitly states these structures are normal based on marker expression, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing pax2.1 expression.

claim: All major retinal cell types are present and the layering of the retina is not affected in kif5aa mutant retinae.
source: Further, cell type specific marker analysis revealed that all major retinal cell types were present and the layering of the retina was not affected in kif5aa mutant retinae (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1E showing immunostaining for different cell types.

claim: No misrouting of RGCs to the ipsilateral side occurs in kif5aa mutants and the optic chiasm is correctly established at the right developmental time.
source: No misrouting of RGCs to the ipsilateral side could be observed, and the optic chiasm was correctly established at the right developmental time (Figure 2A).
evidence: The text explicitly states this observation, supported by Figure 2A showing confocal imaging and Zn5 staining.

claim: The retinotectal projection is correctly patterned in kif5aa mutant embryos.
source: Axon tracing at later stages of development, following injection of the two lipophilic dyes DiO and DiI (Baier et al., 1996) into opposite quadrants of the contralateral eye, revealed that the retinotectal projection was correctly patterned in mutant embryos (Figure 2B) and no misrouting to the ipsilateral hemisphere occurred.
evidence: The text explicitly states this finding based on dye tracing experiments, supported by Figure 2B showing DiI/DiO labeling and citing previous methodology.

claim: Wild-type RGC axons reach the tectal neuropil at 72 hpf and start forming a complex axonal arbor.
source: While wild-type axons reach the tectal neuropil at 72 hpf and start forming a complex axonal arbor, axons of kif5aa mutant RGCs showed a delayed ingrowth into the target tissue (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly describes wild-type axon behavior, supported by Figure 3A showing single RGC imaging.

claim: Axons of kif5aa mutant RGCs show a delayed ingrowth into the target tissue.
source: While wild-type axons reach the tectal neuropil at 72 hpf and start forming a complex axonal arbor, axons of kif5aa mutant RGCs showed a delayed ingrowth into the target tissue (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the delayed ingrowth phenotype, supported by Figure 3A showing comparison of wild-type and mutant RGC axons.

claim: The delayed ingrowth phenotype in kif5aa mutants was confirmed by analyzing a larger RGC population labeled by DiI injections.
source: This phenotype was confirmed by analyzing a larger RGC population, which was labeled by DiI injections into quadrants of the contralateral retina (Figure 3A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the confirmation using DiI labeling, supported by Figure 3A showing DiI-labeled axons.

claim: The vertigos1614 allele co-segregates with the two polymorphic markers fj61a10 and tsub1g3 located on Contig 963 of linkage group 9.
source: In 1800 meioses, the vertigos1614 allele was co-segregating with the two polymorphic markers fj61a10 and tsub1g3 located on Contig 963 of linkage group 9 (LG9).
evidence: The text explicitly states the genetic linkage data, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing the genetic map.

claim: The kif5aa*162 allele does not complement the vertigos1614 allele.
source: In complementation crosses the kif5aa*162 allele was not complementing with the vertigos1614 allele.
evidence: The text explicitly states the complementation test result, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vertigo represents another loss-of-function allele of kif5aa.
source: This strongly suggests that vertigo represents another loss-of-function allele of kif5aa.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on genetic linkage and complementation data.

claim: Between 5 and 7 dpf, kif5aa mutant axons added branches at about double the wild-type rate.
source: Between 5 and 7 dpf, mutant axons added branches at about double the wild-type rate (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: The text explicitly states the branching rate comparison, supported by Figure 3B,C showing time-lapse imaging and quantification.

claim: Kif5aa mutant axons show markedly increased numbers of active filopodia at all time points analyzed.
source: Mutant axons also showed markedly increased numbers of active filopodia either being retracted or newly formed at any time point analyzed, as observed in 10 min timelapse movies (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: The text explicitly describes increased filopodia activity, supported by Figure 3B,D showing tracings and quantification.

claim: Kif5aa mutant RGC axons grow significantly more branches, cover a larger area of the optic tectum with their arbors, and grow longer arbors than wild-type cells at 7 dpf.
source: Kif5aa mutant RGC axons grow significantly more branches, cover a larger area of the optic tectum with their arbors (in μm2) and grow longer arbors (in μm) than wild-type cells at 7 dpf (n = 10, p < 0.01).
evidence: The text explicitly states the quantitative differences with statistical significance, supported by Figure 3C showing measurements.

claim: Wild-type RGC arbors form most filopodia at 3 dpf and reduce this rate constantly until 7 dpf.
source: While wild-type RGC arbors form most filopodia at 3 dpf and reduce this rate constantly until 7 dpf, kif5aa mutant RGC axons grow almost three times more filopodia at 5 dpf (n = 4, p < 0.01).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the temporal pattern of filopodia formation in wild-type, supported by Figure 3D showing quantification over time.

claim: Kif5aa mutant RGC axons grow almost three times more filopodia at 5 dpf compared to wild-type.
source: While wild-type RGC arbors form most filopodia at 3 dpf and reduce this rate constantly until 7 dpf, kif5aa mutant RGC axons grow almost three times more filopodia at 5 dpf (n = 4, p < 0.01).
evidence: The text explicitly states the quantitative comparison with statistical significance, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: At 7 dpf, the filopodia formation rate in kif5aa mutants is still more than double that of wild-type counterparts.
source: At 7 dpf, the rate is still more as double as high as for their wild-type counterparts (n = 4, p < 0.01).
evidence: The text explicitly states the quantitative comparison with statistical significance, supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Clear stimulus-evoked Ca2+ transients were observed in the wild-type PVN layer and tectal neuropil in response to a bar moving in a caudal-to-rostral direction.
source: We did observe clear stimulus-evoked Ca2+ transients in the wild-type PVN layer and the tectal neuropil (the later contains both PVNs dendritic and RGC axonal arbors) in response to a bar (Nikolaou et al., 2012) moving in a caudal-to-rostral direction (Figure 4C, Video 1) across the larva's visual field.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the calcium imaging results, supported by Figure 4C showing deltaF/F0 traces and citing previous methodology.

claim: The visual stimulus response was almost completely absent in kif5aa mutants at 5 dpf.
source: This response was almost completely absent in kif5aa mutants at 5 dpf (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states the absence of response, supported by Figure 4C showing deltaF/F0 traces and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing regression analysis.

claim: No response was detected in kif5aa mutants at 7 dpf, arguing against a delayed onset of activity.
source: In addition, also no response was detected in older larvae (7 dpf), arguing against a delayed onset of activity in mutants, as could have been speculated based on the observed developmental delay of RGC ingrowth (Figure 3).
evidence: The text explicitly states the absence of response at 7 dpf and provides reasoning.

claim: Mutant RGC axons in the tectal neuropil remained unresponsive to visual stimulation, whereas wild-type axons were robustly activated.
source: Mutant RGC axons in the tectal neuropil remained unresponsive to visual stimulation, whereas wild-type axons were robustly activated (Figure 4D).
evidence: The text explicitly states the comparison of responses, supported by Figure 4D showing deltaF/F0 traces for RGC-specific GCaMP3 expression.

claim: The Kif5aa motor is required for proper synaptic transmission from RGC axon terminals to tectal dendrites.
source: These data provide an explanation for the behavioral blindness of kif5aa mutant larvae and indicate that the Kif5aa motor is required for proper synaptic transmission from RGC axon terminals to tectal dendrites.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the calcium imaging results.

claim: No difference in distribution of stable presynaptic clusters was observed between wild-type and kif5aa mutant RGCs at 5 and 7 dpf.
source: When co-expressed with a membrane-localized red fluorescent protein (RFPCaax) in single RGCs in wild-type or kif5aa mutant embryos (Figure 5A), we observed no difference in distribution of stable presynaptic clusters at 5 and 7 dpf by in vivo imaging (Figure 5B).
evidence: The text explicitly states no difference was observed, supported by Figure 5A,B showing Synaptophysin-GFP distribution and quantification.

claim: The formation of stable presynaptic clusters is not affected by the loss of Kif5aa.
source: This indicates that the formation of stable presynaptic clusters is not affected by the loss of Kif5aa.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the Synaptophysin-GFP imaging results.

claim: Quantification of Synaptophysin-containing vesicle movements in axonal segments did not show a difference in either anterograde or retrograde transport upon loss of kif5aa at 4, 5, and 7 dpf.
source: Quantification of Synaptophysin-containing vesicle movements in axonal segments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Video 3) did not show a difference in either anterograde or retrograde transport upon loss of kif5aa at 4, 5, and 7 dpf.
evidence: The text explicitly states no difference in transport, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing kymograph analysis.

claim: Synaptophysin containing vesicles are not transported by Kinesin I.
source: This is consistent with previous studies showing that Synaptophysin containing vesicles are not transported by Kinesin I (Karle et al., 2012) and furthermore argues against a general loss of vesicle movement in kif5aa mutant RGCs.
evidence: The text explicitly states this consistency with previous work and cites the reference.

claim: A higher fraction of small, motile Synaptophysin clusters was detected in kif5aa mutant cells at 4 and 5 dpf, but not at 7 dpf.
source: Using these different categories, we detected a higher fraction of small, motile clusters in kif5aa mutant cells at 4 and 5 dpf, but not at 7 dpf, most probably reflecting their highly active growth behavior at that stage of development (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the temporal pattern of small cluster abundance, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1C showing quantification.

claim: In vivo imaging of labeled mitochondria showed a reduction of mitochondria within the axon of mutant RGCs compared to wild-type cells.
source: In vivo imaging of labeled mitochondria (mitoGFP) and membranes (RFPCaax) in single RGCs in contrast showed a reduction of mitochondria within the axon of mutant RGCs compared to wild-type cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The text explicitly states the reduction, supported by Figure 5C showing mitoGFP distribution in RGC axons.

claim: Mitochondria are transported by Kif5a in other experimental systems.
source: This is consistent with previous reports showing that mitochondria are transported by Kif5a in other experimental systems (Macaskill et al., 2009; Karle et al., 2012; Chen and Sheng, 2013).
evidence: The text explicitly states this consistency with previous work and cites multiple references.

claim: At 6 dpf, kif5aa mutants show a significant depletion of mitochondria from their branched axons.
source: At 6 dpf, mutants show a significant depletion of mitochondria from their branched axons (Figure 5E).
evidence: The text explicitly states the significant depletion, supported by Figure 5E showing quantification of mitochondria area per neuropil area from electron microscopy.

claim: No difference in overall amount of mobile vs stable mitochondria was detected between wild-type and kif5aa mutant RGCs.
source: We did not detect a difference in overall amount of mobile vs stable mitochondria.
evidence: The text explicitly states no difference was detected, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2D showing quantification.

claim: In kif5aa mutant cells, mitochondria were transported significantly more often in a retrograde direction than in an anterograde direction.
source: In mutant cells, though, mitochondria were transported significantly more often in a retrograde direction than in an anterograde direction (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The text explicitly states the directional bias with statistical significance, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2D,E showing quantification.

claim: The bias towards retrograde transport of mitochondria explains the depletion of mitochondria from the tips of kif5aa mutant RGCs.
source: This bias explains the depletion of mitochondria from the tips of kif5aa mutant RGCs.
evidence: The text explicitly states this explanation based on the transport directionality data.

claim: Approximately 40% of stable presynaptic sites are associated with mitochondria in wild-type and blu−/− RGC axons.
source: By co-labeling mitochondria and presynaptic clusters in the same cells in vivo we showed that approximately 40% stable presynaptic sites are associated with mitochondria in wild-type and blu−/− RGC axons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The text explicitly states the percentage, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B showing colocalization analysis.

claim: In TGCs in kif5aa−/−, a marked decrease of presynaptic densities located in close proximity of mitochondria was observed.
source: In contrast to wild-type cells, in TGCs in kif5aa−/− we observed a marked decrease of presynaptic densities located in close proximity of mitochondria.
evidence: The text explicitly states the observation, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B showing TGC analysis.

claim: A recent study in zebrafish reported a reduced number of mitochondria in peripheral cutaneous axon arbors in kif5aa mutant zebrafish embryos without affecting the distribution of presynaptic densities.
source: This observation is consistent with a recent study in zebrafish reporting a reduced number of mitochondria in peripheral cutaneous axon arbors in kif5aa mutant zebrafish embryos (Campbell et al., 2014) without affecting the distribution of presynaptic densities.
evidence: The text explicitly states the consistency with a recent study and cites the reference.

claim: Kif5aa mutant RGCs form presynaptic sites at the same density as wild-type cells.
source: Taken together, these experiments show that kif5aa mutant RGCs form presynaptic sites at the same density as wild-type cells and transport Synaptophysin-containing clusters at the same rate and direction as wild-type.
evidence: The text explicitly summarizes this finding based on the Synaptophysin experiments.

claim: A detectable reduction in the relative anterograde transport of mitochondria results in a depletion of these organelles from synaptic terminals in kif5aa mutants.
source: A detectable reduction in the relative anterograde transport of mitochondria, however, results in a depletion of these organelles from synaptic terminals.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the mitochondria transport and distribution data.

claim: Comparing 4 dpf old homozygous kif5aa mutants to their siblings, a significant upregulation of ntf3 to up to 160% of its normal expression level in wild-type embryos was detected.
source: Comparing 4 dpf old homozygous kif5aa mutants to their siblings, we detected a significant upregulation of ntf3 in mutants to up to 160% of its normal expression level in wild-type embryos, while the levels of bdnf, ngf, ntf4, and ntf7 were not significantly altered (Figure 6A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the upregulation with percentage, supported by Figure 6A showing qRT-PCR data.

claim: The levels of bdnf, ngf, ntf4, and ntf7 were not significantly altered in kif5aa mutants compared to wild-type.
source: Comparing 4 dpf old homozygous kif5aa mutants to their siblings, we detected a significant upregulation of ntf3 in mutants to up to 160% of its normal expression level in wild-type embryos, while the levels of bdnf, ngf, ntf4, and ntf7 were not significantly altered (Figure 6A).
evidence: The text explicitly states no significant alteration for these neurotrophic factors, supported by Figure 6A showing qRT-PCR data.

claim: In situ hybridization showed an increased staining intensity for ntf3 in mutant tecta compared to their siblings.
source: By in situ hybridization with an ntf3 antisense probe, we could furthermore see an increased staining intensity in mutant tecta compared to their siblings (Figure 6B).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the increased staining, supported by Figure 6B showing in situ hybridization images.

claim: Kif5aa mutant embryos produced significantly more Ntf3 protein than their siblings.
source: This experiment showed that kif5aa mutant embryos produced significantly more Ntf3 protein than their siblings.
evidence: The text explicitly states the increased protein production, supported by Figure 6C,D showing Western blot analysis.

claim: Ntf3 protein was increased in the tecta of lakritz and blumenkohl mutant lines in which presynaptic input to the tectum was abolished or highly reduced.
source: Ntf3 protein was increased in the tecta of all three mutant lines in which presynaptic input to the tectum was abolished or highly reduced (Figure 6D).
evidence: The text explicitly states the increase in multiple mutant lines, supported by Figure 6C,D showing Western blot analysis.

claim: Silencing of RGCs via BoTx expression leads to melanosomes expansion and failure to adapt to a light background.
source: Similar to what previously observed in kif5aa, lak, and blu mutants, silencing of RGCs via BoTx expression leads to melanosomes expansion and failure to adapt to a light background (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the phenotype, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1A showing images of BoTx-expressing larvae.

claim: Both via qRT-PCR and Western blotting analysis, an upregulation of Ntf3 was detected in BoTx-expressing transgenic animals.
source: Both, via qRT-PCR and Western blotting analysis we detected an upregulation of Ntf3 in these transgenic animals showing that, like in the previously described mutants, lack of RGCs presynaptic activity per se is sufficient to cause Ntf3 overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The text explicitly states the upregulation detected by both methods, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C showing qRT-PCR and Western blot data.

claim: Lack of RGCs presynaptic activity per se is sufficient to cause Ntf3 overexpression.
source: Both, via qRT-PCR and Western blotting analysis we detected an upregulation of Ntf3 in these transgenic animals showing that, like in the previously described mutants, lack of RGCs presynaptic activity per se is sufficient to cause Ntf3 overexpression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on the BoTx experiment results.

claim: Lack of presynaptic activity and subsequent overexpression of Ntf3 in the tectum trigger the increased size of axonal branches of RGCs in kif5aa, blumenkohl, and lakritz mutants.
source: These results strongly suggest that lack of presynaptic activity and subsequent overexpression of Ntf3 in the tectum trigger the increased size of axonal branches of RGCs in kif5aa, blumenkohl, and lakritz mutants (see Figure 2, [Smear et al., 2007; Gosse et al., 2008]).
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion and cites previous work on blumenkohl and lakritz.

claim: Both ntrk3a and ntrk3b are expressed in RGCs.
source: In zebrafish two TrkC paralogues, ntrk3a and ntrk3b exist, which are both expressed in RGCs (Figure 7A).
evidence: The text explicitly states the expression in RGCs, supported by Figure 7A showing in situ hybridization.

claim: Upon overexpression of the truncated ntrk3adN-GFP construct in single wild-type RGCs, a substantial reduction of axon branch length and number of branches was observed at 5 dpf.
source: Upon overexpression of the truncated ntrk3adN-GFP construct in single wild-type RGCs by mosaic DNA expression, we observed a substantial reduction of axon branch length and number of branches at 5 dpf (Figure 7B,E), consistent with a role of Ntrk3 as a branch-promoting receptor.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the reduction, supported by Figure 7B,E showing images and quantification.

claim: Ntrk3adN-GFP expressing wild-type cells are significantly smaller and grow fewer branches at 5 dpf.
source: Ntrk3adN-GFP expressing wild-type cells are significantly smaller and grow fewer branches at 5 dpf (p < 0.001).
evidence: The text explicitly states the quantitative differences with statistical significance, supported by Figure 7E showing quantification.

claim: In both kif5aa and blumenkohl mutant embryos, expression of ntrk3adN-GFP in single RGCs inhibits the overgrowth of the axonal arbor that is normally observed.
source: In both, kif5aa and blumenkohl mutant embryos, expression of ntrk3adN-GFP in single RGCs inhibits the overgrowth of the axonal arbor that is normally observed.
evidence: The text explicitly states the inhibition of overgrowth, supported by Figure 7E showing quantification.

claim: Ntf3 overexpression in the tectum leads to increased axonal branch length and increased branch number in wild-type RGCs.
source: Ntf3 overexpression in the tectum leads to increased axonal branch length and increased branch number in wild-type RGCs (p < 0.05) (n = 8, 23, 7, 8, 26).
evidence: The text explicitly states the increases with statistical significance, supported by Figure 7C,E showing images and quantification.

claim: Ntf3 upregulation does not per se affect mitochondria localization.
source: In addition, we observed that the distribution of mitochondria was not significantly altered in blu−/− RGC axons nor was the association with stable presynaptic sites (Figure 5—figure supplements 2B, 3). Together these data suggest that Ntf3 upregulation does not per se affect mitochondria localization.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion based on mitochondria distribution analysis in blumenkohl mutants, supported by Figure 5—figure supplements 2B, 3.

claim: Ntf3 upregulation has no significant effect on filopodia dynamics of RGC axons.
source: In both experimental conditions we did not observe any increase in the filopodia dynamics or RGC axons (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C), excluding the possibility that Ntf3 overexpression has a direct effect on this process.
evidence: The text explicitly states no increase was observed, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing filopodia quantification.

claim: The delayed ingrowth of kif5aa mutant RGC axons in the tectal neuropil is a cell-autonomous effect.
source: First, we could observe that the delayed ingrowth of kif5aa mutant RGC axons in the tectal neuropil is a cell-autonomous effect (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The text explicitly states the cell-autonomous nature, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing transplantation experiments.

claim: When growing in a wild-type environment, kif5aa mutant RGC axons invade the tectal neuropil 1 day later (4 dpf) than wild-type cells.
source: When growing in a wild-type environment, kif5aa mutant RGC axons invade the tectal neuropil 1 day later (4 dpf) than wild-type cells.
evidence: The text explicitly states the timing difference, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing time-lapse imaging.

claim: Arbor size was not increased at 5 or 7 dpf in mutant RGC axons that grow into a wild-type tectum.
source: Second, in contrast to what we observed in mutant larvae, arbor size was not increased at 5 or 7 dpf in mutant RGC axons that grow into a wild-type tectum (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The text explicitly states the lack of increase, supported by Figure 8A,B showing images and quantification.

claim: Mutant RGC arbors growing into a wild-type tectum are significantly smaller than wild-type arbors.
source: Mutant RGC arbors are significantly smaller, similar to those that overexpress ntrk3adN-eGFP (see Figure 7B).
evidence: The text explicitly states the size comparison, supported by Figure 8B showing quantification.

claim: Wild-type cells growing in a kif5aa mutant background show no stalling at 3 dpf and establish a significantly increased axonal arbor at 5 and 7 dpf.
source: Wild-type cells growing in a kif5aa mutant background show the opposite behavior. No stalling at 3 dpf was detected (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and, at 5 and 7 dpf, they established a significantly increased axonal arbor (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: The text explicitly describes the phenotype, supported by Figure 8A,B showing images and quantification, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing timing.

claim: Kif5aa mutant RGC axonal arbors were significantly larger when transplanted into a blu mutant host compared to when transplanted into a wild-type host.
source: In these conditions, kif5aa mutant RGC axonal arbors were significantly larger than when transplanted into a wild-type host (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The text explicitly states the size comparison, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2 showing images and quantification.

claim: A deficit in presynaptic activity enhances the production and release of Ntf3 by tectal neurons.
source: Together, these data suggest a model in which a deficit in presynaptic activity enhances the production and release of Ntf3 by tectal neurons.
evidence: The text explicitly states this model based on the experimental results.

claim: Tectum-derived Ntf3 retrogradely stimulates axonal branching and the addition of presynaptic terminals.
source: Tectum-derived Ntf3, in turn, retrogradely stimulates axonal branching and, thus, the addition of presynaptic terminals (Figure 7C).
evidence: The text explicitly states this mechanism, supported by Figure 7C (which is actually Figure 8C based on the description).

claim: The kif5aa mutation results in mRNA degradation likely by nonsense-mediated decay.
source: The loss-of-function kif5aa allele that we generated disrupts the open reading frame after 122 of 1033aa within the motor domain of the protein and results in mRNA degradation likely by nonsense-mediated decay.
evidence: The text explicitly states the mechanism of mRNA degradation.

claim: No functional Kif5aa protein is expected to be produced in the kif5aa mutant.
source: We therefore expect that no functional Kif5aa protein is produced.
evidence: The text explicitly states this expectation based on the nature of the mutation.

claim: At 3 to 4 dpf, RGC axons devoid of Kif5aa grew more slowly and reached their targets in the tectum with a delay of about 24 hr.
source: At 3 to 4 dpf, RGC axons devoid of Kif5aa grew more slowly and reached their targets in the tectum with a delay of about 24 hr.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the timing of the delay.

claim: Mutant retinotectal synapses did not transmit signals to tectal cells, but were apparently silent, resulting in a complete loss of visual responses.
source: Mutant retinotectal synapses did not transmit signals to tectal cells, but were apparently silent, resulting in a complete loss of visual responses.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the synaptic transmission defect and its consequence.

claim: Both the stalled growth and the synaptic transmission defects were likely a direct consequence of the absence of Kif5aa.
source: Both the stalled growth and the synaptic transmission defects were likely a direct consequence of the absence of Kif5aa.
evidence: The text explicitly states this conclusion.

claim: Some of the known cargoes of mammalian Kif5a are required for normal axon outgrowth.
source: Some of the known cargoes of mammalian Kif5a are required for normal axon outgrowth (Karle et al., 2012; Chen and Sheng, 2013; Schwarz, 2013; Sheng, 2014).
evidence: The text explicitly states this and cites multiple references.

claim: Mitochondrial ATP production is required for synapse assembly.
source: Mitochondrial ATP production is required for synapse assembly (Lee and Peng, 2008), the generation of action potentials (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001) and synaptic transmission (Verstreken et al., 2005).
evidence: The text explicitly states this and cites references for each function.

claim: Synaptic mitochondria maintain and regulate neurotransmission by buffering Ca2+.
source: In addition, synaptic mitochondria maintain and regulate neurotransmission by buffering Ca2+ (Medler and Gleason, 2002; David and Barrett, 2003).
evidence: The text explicitly states this function and cites references.

claim: The mitochondrial deficit can explain the impairment in transmitter release at the presynaptic terminals.
